The *Micchādiṭṭhika Sutta* (Iti 70; PTS It 58) is a discourse found in the third division of the *Itivuttaka* [SuttaCentral]. In this sutta, titled "Having Wrong View" (*Micchādiṭṭhikasutta*), the Buddha testifies that he has personally seen beings reborn into states of woe, unhappy destinations, perdition, and hell in accordance with their wrong views, bodily and verbal misconduct, and abuse of noble ones [SuttaCentral].

Curated parallels recorded on SuttaCentral list no external non-Pali witnesses, and computational analysis via DharmaNexus records no cross-language matches with a score of 10 or greater [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus]. Within the Pali canon, however, DharmaNexus detects extensive text reuse, registering 227 shared passages across 41 texts [DharmaNexus]. Its primary counterpart is the immediately following *Sammādiṭṭhika Sutta* (Iti 71), which mirrors its structure and formulaic core almost entirely (§§0.1–4.1 ↔ §§0.1–4.1) to describe the corresponding positive fate of individuals holding right view [DharmaNexus]. The descriptive formula describing beings reborn according to their kamma and views also shares long textual segments (§§2.1–3.1 and §§4.1–4.2) with prominent discourses in the Four Nikāyas, including the *Devadūta Sutta* (MN 130), the *Mahāsīhanāda Sutta* (MN 12), the *Sāmaññaphala Sutta* (DN 2), the *Dasakanipāta* of the *Aṅguttara Nikāya* (AN 10), and the *Nidāna Saṁyutta* (SN 12) [DharmaNexus].

The text has been translated into multiple modern languages, with SuttaCentral listing eighteen translations across sixteen languages, including an English translation by Bhikkhu Sujato [SuttaCentral]. Passages retrieved from secondary literature do not examine Iti 70 directly, but rather discuss the general doctrinal concept of the person holding wrong view (*micchādiṭṭhika*) or cite analogous stock formulas across other canonical and commentarial texts.
